## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Visāsabhojanajātaka* (Ja 93; also attested as *Vissāsabhojanajātaka*) is a canonical story set at Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha on the subject of taking things on trust [SuttaCentral]. The core narrative concerns a lion whose presence so terrifies grazing cattle that they stop yielding milk [Anandajoti 2010]. To resolve this, a doe (or hare-deer) fond of the lion is coated with poison; when the lion affectionately licks her, he is killed [Anandajoti 2010; Sujato 2011]. The verse reflects upon placing trust where one's heart has devotion, even in one not previously known [Anandajoti 2010]. In ethical discussions of the Jātaka literature, this tale is highlighted as one of the narrative instances where the Bodhisatta is implicated in harming or killing, specifically by encouraging a hunter or herdsman to poison the doe to dispatch the lion [Appleton 2010; Sujato 2011].

Regarding textual parallels and reuse, Bhikkhu K. L. Dhammajoti notes scholarly discussion linking a stanza in the Chinese *Dharmapada* featuring the imagery of a lion and a deer (*siṃhaṃ vā mṛgamātṛkā*) to the verse of Jātaka 93 [Dhammajoti 1995]. DharmaNexus identifies no Pali-internal reuse or cross-language matches scoring 10 or above [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the text across four languages [SuttaCentral].
